title: Ink on new paper (Avot 4:20)
hook: learning young is ink on fresh paper, learning old is ink on erased paper; both write
tomorrow: born without asking. so why do we still answer for it?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Shmuel the Small: rejoice not when your enemy falls. Not even quietly. Today, a different kind of fall: the worry that you're too late to start.

A beginner piano class at the community center, Tuesday night. A row of keyboards. A girl whose feet don't reach the floor plays a scale without looking. Beside her, a man with white hair and reading glasses finds middle C, loses it, finds it again. The teacher says, nice, David, and he laughs at himself. Sooner or later somebody will ask it: isn't he a little late for this? A sage in Avot asked it first, as a riddle.
screen: `A BEGINNER CLASS, TUESDAY NIGHT.` → `MIDDLE C, LOST AND FOUND.` → `ISN'T HE A LITTLE LATE?`

segments.voice: Elisha ben Avuyah asks: one who learns as a child, what is that like? Ink written on new paper. One who learns when old, what is that like? Ink written on erased paper. Erased paper is a page scraped and written on again. It's rougher. The ink spreads; the old marks show. Some readers hear a warning: start young, while the page is clean. Others notice what the saying never says. It never says the erased page refuses the ink. Both still write. A little further on, Rabbi Meir adds his own picture: don't look at the jug, look at what's in it. A new jug can be full of old wine, and an old jug may not even hold new wine. So the jug's age tells you nothing. Open it. Here's the part worth repeating tonight. The Talmud says Elisha himself later left the path, and calls him Acher, the other. And Rabbi Meir, his student, kept learning from him anyway, walking beside him. A used page, and his student still found ink on it worth reading. Back to the piano. The man at the keyboard is writing on a used page. It's slower, and the notes smudge. It's still music.
screen: `NEW PAPER, ERASED PAPER.` · `THE OLD PAGE STILL TAKES INK.` · `LOOK INSIDE THE JUG.` · `ACHER, AND HIS STUDENT.` · then, large: `BOTH STILL WRITE.`

segments.voice: Pick up a pen and something to write on, and switch hands. Write today's line, both still write, slowly, with the hand you hardly use; if there's no pen nearby, trace it on your palm. The letters wobble and the pressure is wrong, and every stroke still lands. For the rest of the sit, just look at it: a line written by a beginner.
Ink on new paper: Elisha ben Avuyah's picture of learning young. Its other half is the one to keep: erased paper takes ink too.
Something to keep from the riddle: both still write, the clean page and the used one. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Jewish study has room for adult beginners: some synagogues and community centers teach Hebrew and text study to adults, and some adults celebrate a bar or bat mitzvah later in life.

original.note: Hebrew: new paper. In the riddle, the old learner's page is erased paper.

trapdoor: what you thought: learn it young, or not at all.
what it means: two pages, one clean and one scraped; the rougher one is harder to write on, and it still takes ink.
what a scholar hears: the speaker is Elisha ben Avuyah, whom the Talmud calls Acher, and whose student Rabbi Meir kept learning from him (Chagigah 15a).

chat.meaning: Elisha ben Avuyah compares new paper and erased paper, and both take ink. Rabbi Meir: look at what's in the jug, not its age.

Elisha ben Avuyah.meaning: a sage of the Mishnah; the Talmud later calls him Acher

Acher.meaning: the other: the Talmud's name for Elisha after he left

Rabbi Meir.meaning: a sage of the Mishnah and Elisha's student

Avot.meaning: Pirkei Avot: the sages' sayings, chapters of the fathers

notes: All of Avot paraphrased. 4:20: Elisha ben Avuyah, learning as a child = ink on new paper; as an old man = ink on erased paper (niyar machuk). The jug saying: most printed texts say Rabbi Meir; some read 'Rabbi'. Confirm attribution and numbering (4:20 / 4:25-27).
Chagigah 15a: Elisha is called Acher; Rabbi Meir continues to learn from him (walking beside him on Shabbat). Told lightly; confirm framing.
